Traffic is always bad in big cities, though generally not much of an issue in the wee hours of the night; but the main issue is to response time is coverage. A fire unit is always stationed somewhere with its crew on standby (they don't roam like EMS or police). As such, fire response is centralized on each station, resulting in longer response times simply due to distance traveled. Generally, the crew works hard to ensure that they minimize their load up time so they can minimize their response. But as the guy in the video said, it can be upwards of several minutes after a fire breaks out before dispatch is even notified. Then it takes dispatch time to rely that info to the truck and crew.

At some point the response time simply becomes untenable, as you've seen, by the time fire services are even contacted a room in a house may be fully involved, by the time they get their other rooms may be as well (which is why having doors between rooms that you can close in the event of a fire is the deciding factor of halting or slowing the spread of a fire), and other stations have to be added. Invariably though, these stations only have a limited range, and the bigger the city, the longer the response.

Not only simply city size, but population size also impacts response times, because fire services also have to respond to medical calls (falls, car accidents, heart problems, time-wasters, etc). So they also have to contend with responding to multiple calls from time to time and often have to triage their response. Often they also don't get all the information they need, and have to call in additional units to assist (ala the eponymous 3-alarm fire, the necessity for multiple fire units to respond to a single call, up to and including multiple municipalities). All of this ties up their time and delays response to the next call.

Last but not least of course, is funding. Fire departments the world around are always limited by city funding, or in the case of towns too small to be able to pay for them, volunteers. Municipalities often overlook the importance of properly funding and staffing their fire departments, leading to short staffing, mismanaged staffing, poor dispatch, and over extended services. Usually equipment is the least of the problems, but all the trucks and turn-out gear in the world doesn't help if there aren't bodies to use them.

For a city the size of London, response times should be on par with New York, who averages 5 minutes from when a call comes in from dispatch to response on scene. But on any given night in a city that size, they have to contend with dozens of medical and injury calls. Odds are they were tied up with something and no one was close enough to get there first, and it simply took someone too long to report the fire. That's another factor to be considered, the disregard for fellow occupants by the people in the area the fire began, more concerned with saving their own butts than anyone else. It could very well be that 15 minutes elapsed before dispatch relayed the alarm call, or really any combination of events there of.

Ultimately only the crew on the first truck and the dispatcher could tell you for certain.
